h: Armstrong's Playground of Water and Light
p: William Armstrong was a Tyneside powerhouse. His firm built guns, ships and hydraulic cranes, and he designed the hydraulic machinery for Newcastle's famous Swing Bridge. At Cragside he turned that genius on his own home, with lakes and dams feeding water to power everything from a hydraulic lift to a rotating spit in the kitchen. His friend Joseph Swan supplied the light bulbs that made the house glow. The architect Richard Norman Shaw transformed the original hunting lodge into the dramatic house you see now.

Out on the estate, look for the Power House and the Ram House, where you can learn how the water was harnessed. The Iron Bridge spanning the Debdon Burn is one of the most photographed spots, and the pinetum is home to some seriously tall conifers. There's also a woodland labyrinth for children who enjoy getting a bit lost.

You can drive the long Carriage Drive in stages, stopping at different car parks for short walks, which is handy for anyone who can't manage the steeper paths. Allow a full day if you want to see the house and explore properly.

Rothbury makes a smashing base for exploring Coquetdale. The Simonside Hills, part of Northumberland National Park, rise just south of the town and offer cracking walks with big views. Brinkburn Priory, a beautifully restored medieval church by the River Coquet, is a short drive away, and Alnwick, with its castle and famous gardens, is around half an hour away by car.
